source.name: OER Commons open software testing & QA curriculum

course.title: Software Testing & QA
course.description: Learn to prove your code works and keep it working - unit tests, test-driven development, test doubles, coverage, bug reporting, continuous integration, and non-functional testing, ending in a full test plan. Structure adapted from open software testing and quality-assurance curricula on OER Commons (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: In the testing pyramid, which layer should have the most tests?
questions.explanation: The pyramid is wide at the bottom: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few slow end-to-end tests - see 'Why testing matters and the testing pyramid'.

questions.prompt: The three parts of a well-structured unit test are best described as...
questions.explanation: Arrange the inputs, act by calling the code under test, then assert the result - see 'Unit testing'.

questions.prompt: Test-driven development follows which cycle?
questions.explanation: You write a failing test (red), make it pass (green), then clean up the code (refactor).

questions.prompt: A fake object that records how it was called so the test can check those calls is a...
questions.explanation: A mock verifies interactions; a stub only feeds back canned answers - see 'Test doubles'.

questions.prompt: 100% line coverage guarantees that...
options: every line ran at least once during tests
questions.explanation: Coverage measures which lines executed, not whether behavior is correct - see 'Coverage'.

questions.prompt: Testing the values just below, at, and just above a limit like 0 to 100 is called...
questions.explanation: Bugs cluster at edges, so you probe the boundaries - see 'Writing good test cases'.

questions.prompt: A good bug report should always include...
options: steps to reproduce, expected result, and actual result
questions.explanation: Reproduction steps plus expected versus actual behavior let anyone confirm and diagnose the bug.

questions.prompt: Continuous integration means that...
options: code is deployed once a year
tests run automatically when changes are pushed
tests are run by hand before release
questions.explanation: CI runs the test suite on every push so problems are caught within minutes.

lessons.title: Why testing matters and the testing pyramid
lessons.grammar_note: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change is called flaky - fix or delete it, never ignore it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why automated tests pay for themselves, and place a test in the right layer of the testing pyramid. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which layer of the pyramid should hold the most tests?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A test is code that checks other code and fails loudly when behavior is wrong. Tests matter because the cost of a bug grows the later you catch it: a mistake caught while typing costs seconds, the same mistake caught by a user in production can cost hours and trust. Automated tests give you a fast feedback loop and a safety net, so you can change code without fear. The testing pyramid organizes tests by scope and speed. The wide base is unit tests: tiny, fast, and isolated, checking one function at a time. The middle is integration tests: a few pieces working together, such as code plus a database. The narrow top is end-to-end tests: the whole system driven like a real user, which are valuable but slow and brittle. Aim for many unit tests, some integration tests, and a few end-to-end tests. The opposite shape - mostly slow end-to-end tests with almost no unit tests - is the 'ice cream cone' anti-pattern, and it produces test suites that are slow and painful to maintain.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Suppose you have a function total_price(cart) that sums item prices and adds tax. A unit test calls it directly with a small cart and asserts the returned number, running in under a millisecond. An integration test might save an order to a real test database and read it back to confirm the total was stored. An end-to-end test would open the checkout page in a browser, click through, and verify the on-screen total. All three are useful, but if you have 400 tests, a healthy split is roughly 320 unit, 60 integration, and 20 end-to-end - fast tests you run constantly, slow tests you run sparingly.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which is faster to run, a unit test or an end-to-end test? 2) Name the three layers of the pyramid from bottom to top. 3) A test opens a browser and clicks the real Buy button - which layer is that? 4) What is the ice cream cone anti-pattern? 5) Why does a bug cost more the later it is found? Answers: 1) A unit test - it touches one function with no browser or database. 2) Unit, integration, end-to-end. 3) End-to-end. 4) A suite that is mostly slow end-to-end tests with too few unit tests, the pyramid upside down. 5) More code and more users depend on it, so diagnosis and repair take longer and the damage is wider.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing only end-to-end tests because they feel realistic - they are slow, flaky, and hard to debug when they fail. Mistake: treating a passing suite as proof of zero bugs; tests only check the cases you thought to write. Exit: (a) Which layer of the pyramid should be widest? (b) What do we call a test that passes and fails randomly with no code change? Answers: the unit layer; a flaky test.

lessons.title: Unit testing: arrange, act, assert
lessons.grammar_note: One test should check one behavior - if a test needs the word 'and' to describe it, it is probably two tests.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write a clear unit test using the arrange-act-assert structure and choose the right assertion. Warm-up: what are the three phases every unit test moves through?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A unit test isolates one small piece of behavior and checks it. The arrange-act-assert pattern keeps tests readable: arrange sets up the inputs and any needed state, act performs the single action under test, and assert compares the result to what you expect. An assertion is the check that decides pass or fail: assert_equal(actual, expected) passes when they match, and there are also assert_true, assert_false, assert_raises for expected errors, and assert_almost_equal for floating-point numbers. A test has one reason to fail, a descriptive name, and no dependence on other tests or on the order they run in.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: For a function add(a, b): test add_two_positive_numbers() - arrange: a = 2, b = 3; act: result = add(2, 3); assert: assert_equal(result, 5). For a function that should reject bad input, test that it raises: arrange a negative age; act and assert together with assert_raises(ValueError): set_age(-1). A floating-point case avoids exact equality: assert_almost_equal(total_price([0.1, 0.2]), 0.30, places=2), because 0.1 + 0.2 is not stored as exactly 0.3. Naming matters: test_empty_cart_total_is_zero() tells you instantly what broke when it fails, while test1() tells you nothing.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three phases of arrange-act-assert. 2) Which assertion checks that calling a function throws an error? 3) Why avoid assert_equal for the result of 0.1 + 0.2? 4) Rewrite the test name 'test2' into something useful for a function is_even. 5) True or false: a good unit test may depend on another test running first. Answers: 1) Arrange, act, assert. 2) assert_raises (or its equivalent, sometimes assert_throws). 3) Floating-point rounding means the result is not exactly 0.3, so use assert_almost_equal. 4) For example test_is_even_returns_true_for_four. 5) False - tests must be independent and order-free.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: putting several unrelated assertions in one test, so a failure does not tell you which behavior broke. Mistake: sharing state between tests, which creates failures that appear only in a certain run order. Exit: (a) In arrange-act-assert, which phase calls the code under test? (b) Which assertion suits comparing floating-point results? Answers: the act phase; assert_almost_equal.

lessons.title: Test-driven development: red, green, refactor
lessons.grammar_note: In test-driven development you are never allowed to write production code unless a failing test demands it - the failing test comes first.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Drive a small feature through the red-green-refactor cycle and explain why writing the test first changes your design. Warm-up: in test-driven development, which do you write first, the test or the code?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Test-driven development (TDD) reverses the usual order: you write a failing test before the code that makes it pass. The cycle has three steps. Red: write the smallest test for the next bit of behavior and watch it fail, proving the test actually checks something. Green: write the simplest code that makes the test pass, even if it is ugly. Refactor: with the test as a safety net, clean up names and structure while keeping every test green. You repeat this loop in tiny increments. Writing the test first forces you to describe the desired behavior before the implementation, which tends to produce simpler interfaces and code that is testable by design.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Build a function fizzbuzz(n). Red: write test_returns_number_as_string_by_default - assert_equal(fizzbuzz(1), '1'). It fails because fizzbuzz does not exist. Green: define fizzbuzz(n): return str(n). Test passes. Red again: test_multiple_of_three_returns_fizz - assert_equal(fizzbuzz(3), 'Fizz'). It fails. Green: add if n % 3 == 0: return 'Fizz' before the return. Red again: test_multiple_of_five_returns_buzz expecting 'Buzz', then handle n % 5 == 0. Red again: test_multiple_of_fifteen_returns_fizzbuzz expecting 'FizzBuzz', then handle n % 15 == 0 first. Refactor: notice the checks can be ordered fifteen, three, five, and tidy the branches - the four tests stay green, proving you did not break anything.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What are the three steps of the cycle, in order? 2) Why do you run the test and watch it fail before writing code? 3) During refactor, what must stay true of every test? 4) In the fizzbuzz build, why check n % 15 before n % 3? 5) True or false: in TDD you write all the tests first, then all the code. Answers: 1) Red, green, refactor. 2) To confirm the test can fail, so a later pass actually means something. 3) They must all still pass (stay green). 4) A multiple of 15 is also a multiple of 3, so the 15 case must win first or you would never see 'FizzBuzz'. 5) False - you alternate one small test and its code at a time.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing a big test that forces a big chunk of code, which loses the tight feedback loop. Mistake: skipping the refactor step, so the code passes but rots. Exit: (a) Which color means 'a failing test'? (b) What is the goal of the refactor step? Answers: red; to improve the code's structure while keeping all tests green.

lessons.title: Integration and end-to-end testing
lessons.grammar_note: The more real pieces a test wires together, the more it tells you and the slower and flakier it gets - spend that cost deliberately.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell integration tests from end-to-end tests, and decide what each should cover. Warm-up: which kind of test drives the whole app the way a real user would?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Unit tests check one piece in isolation, but real systems fail at the seams. An integration test checks that two or more components work together - for example your code plus a real database, or your service calling another service. It confirms wiring, data formats, and contracts that a unit test with fake inputs cannot see. An end-to-end (E2E) test goes further and exercises the entire system from the outside, usually by driving the user interface: it fills a form, clicks a button, and checks what appears. E2E tests catch problems no smaller test can, but they are slow, need a running environment, and break easily when the interface changes, so you keep only a few that cover the most important paths - often called the critical path or 'happy path'.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Integration test of a repository layer: arrange a real test database; act by calling save_user({name: 'Ada'}) then load_user_by_name('Ada'); assert the loaded record's name equals 'Ada'. This proves your SQL and mapping actually round-trip, which a unit test with a fake store would miss. End-to-end test of checkout, written in a browser-driving style: open('/shop'); click('Add to cart'); click('Checkout'); fill('card', '4111...'); click('Pay'); assert_text_visible('Order confirmed'). If any layer between the page and the database is broken, this single test fails - but it takes seconds, not milliseconds, so you might run it only in continuous integration rather than on every save.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which test type drives the real user interface end to end? 2) Give one failure an integration test catches that a unit test cannot. 3) Why keep only a few end-to-end tests? 4) What is the 'happy path'? 5) Why use a separate test database rather than the production one? Answers: 1) The end-to-end test. 2) A mismatch between the code and the real database schema or query - a seam a unit test with fakes never touches. 3) They are slow and brittle, so many of them make the suite painful. 4) The main successful flow a typical user takes, with no errors. 5) To avoid corrupting real data and to let tests create and delete freely.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trying to cover every edge case through the user interface, producing a huge slow E2E suite - push edge cases down to unit tests. Mistake: sharing one database between tests so leftover data makes results depend on order. Exit: (a) What does an integration test verify that a unit test does not? (b) Name one downside of end-to-end tests. Answers: that separate components actually work together (real wiring, formats, contracts); they are slow and brittle.

questions.prompt: The widest layer of the testing pyramid, run most often, is...
questions.explanation: Unit tests are fast and isolated, so you keep many and run them constantly.

questions.prompt: In arrange-act-assert, the phase that calls the code under test is...
questions.explanation: Act performs the single action; arrange sets up, assert checks.

questions.prompt: For a result that might be 0.30000000000000004, the safest assertion is...
questions.explanation: Floating-point rounding means exact equality can fail; compare to a tolerance.

questions.prompt: In red-green-refactor, 'green' means...
questions.explanation: Green is the step where you write the simplest code that makes the failing test pass.

questions.prompt: A test that saves to a real database and reads the record back is a...
questions.explanation: It checks that two components - code and database - work together.

questions.prompt: Why keep end-to-end tests few in number?
questions.explanation: E2E tests are valuable but slow and easily broken by interface changes, so cover only critical paths.

lessons.title: Test doubles: mocks, stubs, and fakes
lessons.grammar_note: A stub answers questions, a mock also checks that it was asked - use a mock only when the interaction itself is the behavior you want to verify.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Replace a slow or unpredictable dependency with the right kind of test double, and know when a mock is overkill. Warm-up: why would you not want a unit test to send a real email?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A test double is any stand-in you swap in for a real dependency so a test stays fast, isolated, and deterministic. The common kinds: a stub returns canned answers so your code has something to work with (for example a stub that always returns a fixed exchange rate). A mock is a stub that also records how it was called, so the test can assert that a certain method was invoked with certain arguments. A fake is a lightweight working implementation - such as an in-memory dictionary standing in for a database - real enough to use but not production-grade. A spy wraps a real object and records calls to it. Reach for stubs and fakes by default; use mocks sparingly, only when the interaction (that a message was sent) is the behavior under test, because tests full of mocks become tightly coupled to how the code works rather than what it does.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Stub: testing checkout, you do not want a live payment network, so stub it - payment = StubGateway(always_succeeds=True); the test controls the outcome. Mock: you must prove that placing an order sends a confirmation, so use a mock - mailer = Mock(); place_order(cart, mailer); assert mailer.send was called once with to='ada@example.com'. Here the sending is the behavior, so verifying the call is correct. Fake: instead of a real database, inject an in-memory store - repo = FakeUserRepo() backed by a dictionary - so save and load work in memory with no setup. Contrast with a stub-only version: if you merely stub load_user to return a fixed user, you are not testing that save actually persisted anything.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which double records the calls made to it so you can assert on them? 2) Which double is a simple working implementation, like an in-memory database? 3) Why not send real emails in a unit test? 4) When is a mock the right choice? 5) What is the risk of overusing mocks? Answers: 1) A mock. 2) A fake. 3) It is slow, needs a network, and has real side effects outside your control. 4) When the interaction itself - that a method was called with certain arguments - is the behavior you need to verify. 5) Tests become coupled to the implementation, so refactoring breaks them even when behavior is unchanged.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: mocking everything, which turns a test into a mirror of the code and hides real bugs. Mistake: using a mock when a stub would do - if you never assert on the calls, you did not need a mock. Exit: (a) What distinguishes a mock from a stub? (b) Name a good use for a fake. Answers: a mock records and lets you verify how it was called; a fake gives a fast in-memory replacement for something like a database.

lessons.title: Coverage: what it does and does not tell you
lessons.grammar_note: Coverage is a floor, not a goal - it can only tell you what was not run, never that what ran was correct.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a coverage report, tell line coverage from branch coverage, and explain why 100% coverage is not the same as correctness. Warm-up: if every line ran during your tests, does that prove the program has no bugs?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Code coverage measures how much of your code was executed while the tests ran. Line coverage is the percent of lines that ran at least once. Branch coverage is stricter: it asks whether each direction of every if - both the true and the false path - was taken. Coverage is useful because it points at code no test touches, which is code you cannot trust. But it is easy to misread. High coverage does not mean the assertions are meaningful: a test can run a line and check nothing. And coverage says nothing about inputs you never tried. Treat coverage as a way to find blind spots, not as a score to maximize; chasing 100% often produces low-value tests that exist only to touch a line.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Consider: def classify(n): if n > 0: return 'positive' else: return 'nonpositive'. A single test classify(5) gives 100% line coverage of the returns it reaches but misses the else branch entirely - branch coverage would be 50%, revealing the gap. Add classify(-1) and branch coverage reaches 100%. A subtler trap: a test that calls classify(5) but forgets to assert the result still counts as covering those lines, so the report looks green while checking nothing. And even at 100% branch coverage, classify(0) shows the boundary behavior returns 'nonpositive' - coverage told you the branch ran, not whether that answer is what you wanted.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does line coverage measure? 2) How is branch coverage stricter? 3) Can a test raise coverage without checking anything? 4) Does 100% coverage prove there are no bugs? 5) A function has one if statement; a single test only hits the true side - what is its branch coverage? Answers: 1) The percent of lines executed at least once during tests. 2) It requires both the true and false side of each decision to be exercised, not just each line. 3) Yes - running a line with no assertion still counts as covered. 4) No - it only shows what ran, not that the results were correct or that all inputs were tried. 5) 50%, because the false branch never ran.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: setting a coverage target so high that developers write hollow tests just to hit lines. Mistake: reading green coverage as a guarantee of quality when the tests may assert nothing. Exit: (a) What kind of coverage checks both sides of every if? (b) Name one thing coverage cannot tell you. Answers: branch coverage; whether the behavior is correct (or which untested inputs still break it).

lessons.title: Writing good test cases: equivalence classes and boundary values
lessons.grammar_note: You cannot test every input, so test one representative from each group and then hammer the edges between groups.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Design a small but strong set of test cases using equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis. Warm-up: for an input that must be 1 to 100, which exact values would you be most suspicious of?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: You can never try every possible input, so you choose inputs cleverly. Equivalence partitioning splits the input space into groups that the code should treat the same way, then tests one representative from each - if 50 is handled correctly, 51 probably is too. The groups usually include valid inputs and several kinds of invalid inputs. Boundary value analysis then targets the edges of each group, because off-by-one errors live there: for a valid range of 1 to 100, you test 0 (just below), 1 (the low edge), 100 (the high edge), and 101 (just above), plus a middle value like 50. Together these two techniques give you a handful of high-value cases instead of thousands of redundant ones. Do not forget the ugly inputs: empty, zero, negative, very large, and wrong type.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A function grade(score) accepts 0 to 100 and returns a letter. Equivalence classes: below range (score < 0, should error), valid (0 to 100), above range (score > 100, should error). Representatives: -5, 55, 150. Boundary values around the valid range: -1, 0, 100, 101. So a strong minimal suite is roughly: grade(-1) errors, grade(0) is valid, grade(100) is valid, grade(101) errors, grade(55) is a middle valid case. Another example, a password length rule of 8 to 64 characters: test lengths 7, 8, 64, 65, and one comfortably valid length like 20 - five tests that catch nearly every off-by-one and range mistake, versus checking every length from 1 to 100.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is an equivalence class? 2) For a valid range 1 to 100, list the four boundary values worth testing. 3) Why test one value per class instead of many? 4) Name three 'ugly' inputs worth always trying. 5) A field allows 3 to 20 characters - which lengths would you test? Answers: 1) A group of inputs the code should treat the same, so one represents all. 2) 0, 1, 100, 101. 3) The class members behave the same, so extra ones add cost without new information. 4) For example empty, zero or negative, and very large or wrong type. 5) 2, 3, 20, 21, and a comfortable middle like 10.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: testing only tidy valid inputs and never the boundaries or the invalid classes, where most bugs hide. Mistake: piling on many inputs from the same class, which feels thorough but adds no coverage of behavior. Exit: (a) Which technique targets the edges of a range? (b) For a 1 to 100 range, name the two values just outside it. Answers: boundary value analysis; 0 and 101.

questions.prompt: A test double that records how it was called so you can assert on those calls is a...
questions.explanation: A mock verifies interactions; a stub only returns canned values.

questions.prompt: An in-memory dictionary standing in for a real database is best called a...
questions.explanation: A fake is a lightweight but working implementation used in place of the real thing.

questions.prompt: Branch coverage is stricter than line coverage because it requires...
options: both the true and false path of each decision to run
questions.explanation: Branch coverage checks each direction of every if, not just that a line executed.

questions.prompt: A test runs a line but makes no assertion. That line's coverage is...
questions.explanation: Coverage records execution, so the line counts as covered even though nothing was checked - a key limitation.

questions.prompt: For a valid input range of 1 to 100, boundary value analysis would test...
questions.explanation: You probe just below, at, and just above each edge: 0, 1, 100, 101.

questions.prompt: Equivalence partitioning helps you...
options: pick one representative input per group of same-behaving inputs
run tests faster on the server
questions.explanation: You split inputs into classes treated alike, then test one from each.

lessons.title: Bug reporting and the QA process
lessons.grammar_note: A bug report is a handoff document - write it so a stranger can reproduce the problem without asking you a single question.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write a bug report that anyone can act on, and place it in the quality-assurance workflow from discovery to closed. Warm-up: what three facts must every bug report contain?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Quality assurance (QA) is the whole process of building confidence that software meets its requirements - not just running tests, but reporting, triaging, fixing, and verifying. When a defect is found, it is captured in a bug report. A strong report has a clear one-line title, numbered steps to reproduce, the expected result, the actual result, and the environment (version, operating system, browser). It often adds severity (how bad the impact is) and priority (how soon to fix), which are different: a rare crash can be high severity but low priority, while an annoying typo on the home page can be low severity but high priority. The typical lifecycle is: New, then Triaged (confirmed and prioritized), then In Progress, then Fixed, then Verified by QA against the original steps, then Closed - or reopened if the fix did not hold.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A weak report: 'Login is broken.' Nobody can act on it. A strong report: Title - 'Login fails with valid credentials on Safari 17'. Steps: 1) Open /login on Safari 17. 2) Enter a known-good email and password. 3) Click Sign in. Expected: user lands on the dashboard. Actual: page reloads to /login with no error message. Environment: build 2.4.1, macOS, Safari 17. Severity: high (blocks all Safari users). Priority: high. Now anyone can reproduce and diagnose it. On lifecycle: this bug moves New to Triaged (a lead confirms it and tags it high priority), to In Progress (a developer takes it), to Fixed (a change is merged), to Verified (QA reruns the three steps on Safari 17 and reaches the dashboard), to Closed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name three things every bug report must include. 2) How do severity and priority differ? 3) Give an example of high severity but low priority. 4) What does the 'Verified' step involve? 5) Why include the environment in a report? Answers: 1) Steps to reproduce, expected result, actual result (title and environment are also expected). 2) Severity is how damaging the bug is; priority is how urgently it should be fixed. 3) A crash that only happens on a rare, nearly unused configuration. 4) QA reruns the original reproduction steps to confirm the fix actually works. 5) Bugs often depend on version, operating system, or browser, so reproducing needs that context.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: vague titles and missing steps, forcing a back-and-forth before anyone can even reproduce the bug. Mistake: confusing severity with priority and fixing loud-but-harmless issues before quiet-but-critical ones. Exit: (a) Which report field lists exactly how to trigger the bug? (b) Which lifecycle step has QA confirm the fix? Answers: steps to reproduce; Verified.

lessons.title: Automation and continuous integration basics
lessons.grammar_note: If a check matters, automate it - a rule enforced by a machine on every push beats a rule that people are supposed to remember.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a continuous integration pipeline does and sketch a simple one that runs on every change. Warm-up: when should the test suite run - only before a release, or on every push?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Automation means letting a machine run your checks so they happen the same way every time, without anyone remembering to. Continuous integration (CI) is the practice of automatically building and testing every change as soon as it is pushed, so problems surface within minutes rather than at release. A CI pipeline is a list of stages that run in order on a fresh, clean machine: typically install dependencies, run static checks (a linter and formatter), run the unit and integration tests, and measure coverage. If any stage fails, the pipeline goes red and the change is blocked from merging. Because CI starts from a clean environment, it also catches the classic 'works on my machine' bug, where code depends on something only your laptop had. A green pipeline is the shared signal that a change is safe to merge.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A minimal pipeline, written as ordered steps: 1) checkout the code. 2) install dependencies. 3) run the linter (fail on style or obvious errors). 4) run the unit tests. 5) run the integration tests. 6) report coverage and fail if it drops below an agreed floor. Each step must exit successfully for the next to run. In practice this is described in a small configuration file, for example: on: push; steps: [install, lint, test, coverage]. A concrete failure: a developer renames a function but forgets one caller; their local run happened to skip that path, but CI runs the full suite on a clean checkout, the integration test fails, the pipeline turns red, and the merge is blocked until it is fixed - exactly the outcome you want, caught in minutes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does continuous integration automate? 2) Why run the pipeline on a clean machine instead of a developer's laptop? 3) List three stages a typical pipeline runs. 4) What happens to a change when a pipeline stage fails? 5) What does a green pipeline signal to the team? Answers: 1) Building and testing every change automatically as soon as it is pushed. 2) To catch dependencies on local-only setup - the 'works on my machine' problem - and to make runs reproducible. 3) For example install dependencies, lint, and run tests (coverage is another). 4) The pipeline goes red and the change is blocked from merging. 5) That the change built and passed all checks, so it is safe to merge.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: letting flaky tests stay in CI, which trains the team to ignore red pipelines. Mistake: running tests only manually before a release, so bugs pile up unseen for weeks. Exit: (a) When does CI run the test suite? (b) What does a red pipeline stop from happening? Answers: automatically on every push (change); merging the change.

lessons.title: Non-functional testing: performance, accessibility, and security
lessons.grammar_note: Functional tests ask 'does it do the right thing'; non-functional tests ask 'how well does it do it' - both must pass for real quality.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish functional from non-functional testing and describe basic checks for performance, accessibility, and security. Warm-up: a page returns the correct data but takes 30 seconds - which kind of requirement did it fail?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Functional testing checks whether the software produces the correct result. Non-functional testing checks the qualities of how it behaves. Performance testing measures speed and capacity: response time under normal use, and load testing to see how the system holds up as many users arrive at once, watching for slow responses or crashes. Accessibility testing checks that people using assistive technology can use the product: images have text alternatives, forms have labels, color is not the only way meaning is shown, and everything works from the keyboard. Security testing looks for weaknesses attackers could exploit: never trusting user input, checking that untrusted text cannot be run as code (injection), and confirming that users can only reach data they are allowed to. These are easy to forget because a feature can be perfectly correct and still be slow, unusable for some people, or unsafe.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Performance: assert that a search endpoint responds in under 300 milliseconds for a typical query, then run a load test with 500 simultaneous users and assert the error rate stays near zero. Accessibility: check that every image has alt text - assert image.alt is not empty - that each form input has an associated label, and that a keyboard-only user can complete checkout with no mouse. Security: for an input field, feed a hostile value like ' OR '1'='1 and assert the query treats it as plain data, not as part of the command (using parameterized queries); and assert that requesting another user's record without permission returns 'forbidden', not their data. Each of these can fail even when the ordinary functional test - 'search returns the right items' - passes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does load testing measure? 2) Give two things accessibility testing checks. 3) What is the security risk when untrusted input is run as code? 4) Can a feature be functionally correct and still fail non-functional tests? 5) Name the non-functional category for 'the page must load in under one second'. Answers: 1) How the system behaves under many simultaneous users - response time and stability. 2) For example alt text on images, labels on form fields, keyboard access, or not using color alone (any two). 3) Injection, where hostile input is executed instead of treated as data. 4) Yes - it can be correct yet slow, inaccessible, or insecure. 5) Performance.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating accessibility and security as optional extras rather than requirements, so they are never tested. Mistake: measuring performance only on a fast laptop with one user, missing how it behaves under real load. Exit: (a) Which testing category covers assistive-technology support? (b) What is an injection attack in one line? Answers: accessibility testing; when hostile input is executed as code instead of being treated as plain data.

questions.prompt: A bug that only crashes on a rare, barely used configuration is best described as...
questions.explanation: The crash is serious (high severity) but rarely hit, so it can wait (low priority).

questions.prompt: The QA lifecycle step where QA reruns the original steps to confirm a fix is...
questions.explanation: Verified means QA confirmed the fix against the reproduction steps before Closing.

questions.prompt: Continuous integration runs the test suite...
questions.explanation: CI builds and tests every change as soon as it is pushed, catching problems in minutes.

questions.prompt: Running the pipeline on a fresh clean machine mainly catches...
questions.explanation: A clean checkout exposes dependencies on local-only setup that a laptop happened to have.

questions.prompt: Testing that a system stays stable with 500 simultaneous users is...
questions.explanation: Load testing measures behavior under many concurrent users.

questions.prompt: Feeding ' OR '1'='1 into a field to see if it is executed as code tests for...
questions.explanation: It checks that untrusted input is treated as plain data, not run as part of a command.

lessons.title: Capstone: write a test plan
lessons.grammar_note: A test plan is a decision, not a wish list - for each feature you name what you will test, at which layer, and how you will know it passed.

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Produce a written test plan for one small feature of your choosing - for example a login form, a shopping cart, or a temperature converter. The plan should show that you can choose the right kinds of tests at the right layers and justify what you leave out. Aim for something a teammate could pick up and turn into real tests.

sections.heading: The structure to follow
sections.text: 1) Scope: state the feature in one or two sentences and list what is in and out of scope. 2) Unit tests: list the individual functions to test and, for each, the equivalence classes and boundary values you will cover. 3) Integration tests: name the seams that need real components wired together (for example code plus database). 4) End-to-end tests: name the one or two critical user paths worth driving through the interface. 5) Non-functional checks: state at least one performance, one accessibility, and one security check. 6) Exit criteria: state how you will know testing is done - for example all tests green in CI, branch coverage above an agreed floor, and no open high-severity bugs.

sections.heading: A worked model for a different feature
sections.text: Feature: a discount_code(cart_total, code) function that applies a percentage discount for a valid code and rejects invalid ones. Scope: only the calculation, not the checkout page. Unit tests: equivalence classes are valid code, unknown code, and expired code; boundary values include cart_total of 0, a tiny positive amount, and a very large amount; assert discount_code(100, 'SAVE10') returns 90, discount_code(100, 'NOPE') raises an error, and discount_code(0, 'SAVE10') returns 0. Integration test: save and load a code from a real test database and confirm an expired one is rejected. End-to-end test: on the checkout page, apply 'SAVE10' and assert the on-screen total drops by 10 percent. Non-functional: performance - the function returns in under 5 milliseconds; accessibility - the code field has a label and an error is announced, not shown by color alone; security - a code value of ' OR '1'='1 is treated as plain text and simply reported invalid. Exit criteria: all of the above green in CI, branch coverage at least 90 percent, no open high-severity bugs. Use this as a template of depth and structure - do not copy it; write your own plan for your own feature.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check yes to each: the scope names what is in and out; every unit-tested function lists at least one equivalence class and one boundary value; at least one real integration seam is identified; one or two end-to-end critical paths are chosen (not the whole app); there is at least one performance, one accessibility, and one security check; the exit criteria are concrete and measurable (green CI, a coverage floor, no open high-severity bugs). If all six are true, you have written a test plan you could actually hand off.

questions.prompt: The testing pyramid recommends the most tests at which layer?
questions.explanation: Fast, isolated unit tests form the wide base; slow end-to-end tests are the narrow top.

questions.prompt: In arrange-act-assert, which phase performs the single action under test?
questions.explanation: Act calls the code; arrange prepares inputs, assert checks the result.

questions.prompt: The correct order of the test-driven development cycle is...
questions.explanation: Write a failing test (red), make it pass (green), then improve the code (refactor).

questions.prompt: Which test verifies that your code and a real database work together?
questions.explanation: Integration tests exercise the seam between separate components.

questions.prompt: A test double that both returns canned values and lets you assert how it was called is a...
questions.explanation: A mock records interactions so you can verify the calls; a stub only returns values.

questions.prompt: 100% line coverage guarantees which of the following?
options: every line ran at least once
questions.explanation: Coverage only records that lines executed - not correctness or completeness of inputs.

questions.prompt: For an input valid from 1 to 100, boundary value analysis tests...
questions.explanation: You probe just below, at, and just above each edge of the range.

questions.prompt: Severity and priority differ in that...
options: severity is impact, priority is urgency
priority is impact, severity is urgency
both measure how soon to fix
questions.explanation: Severity is how damaging the bug is; priority is how urgently it should be fixed.

questions.prompt: A continuous integration pipeline turns red when...
options: any stage such as lint or tests fails
questions.explanation: If any ordered stage fails, the pipeline goes red and blocks the merge.

questions.prompt: Checking that images have text alternatives and forms have labels is...
questions.explanation: Accessibility testing confirms people using assistive technology can use the product.

questions.prompt: Feeding a hostile value that could be executed as a command tests for...
questions.explanation: Injection testing checks that untrusted input is treated as data, never run as code.

questions.prompt: In a test plan, good exit criteria are...
options: concrete and measurable, like green CI and a coverage floor with no open high-severity bugs
questions.explanation: Exit criteria must be objective so anyone can tell when testing is complete.
